entries.narration: A machine learning model on its own only produces a prediction. An operational system wraps that prediction in an action, an outcome follows from the action, and the product is judged on an objective that may be several steps away from the model's own score. This course follows the retailer from the Machine Learning course, which now runs two separate systems. The checkout predictor scores each order as it is placed. A late-delivery risk of nought point three one leads the checkout page to show a wider delivery window, and whether the parcel actually arrives on time is only known days later. The daily planning job runs overnight, predicts tomorrow's delivery durations, and the logistics team uses them to assign drivers, so its objective is cost per delivery, not prediction error. Throughout the course, four kinds of claim are kept apart, because each needs different evidence. Software correctness is shown by tests and contract checks. Model quality is shown by validation and test metrics. Business utility needs a controlled experiment on the objective itself. And operational health is shown by latency, errors and freshness. Evidence for one never establishes another: a healthy, correct service can still serve a model that makes the product worse.

The same model can sit inside very different systems, so the first engineering step is to write down each system's requirements before choosing any architecture. The checkout predictor is called inside every checkout request, at around forty requests a second at peak, and it must answer within a hundred and fifty milliseconds at the ninety-ninth percentile, because the customer is waiting. The daily planning job scores around a hundred and eighty thousand orders in one run, starting at two in the morning, and has until five to finish, a three-hour window. The inputs differ too. Checkout features must be known at the moment of checkout, while the planning job reads a snapshot of the order tables taken at one o'clock. And so do the failure requirements. If the checkout model fails, checkout itself must keep working, so there has to be a fallback. If the planning job fails, routing falls back to yesterday's plan plus simple rules. Each system also depends on things other teams own: the checkout API, the feature service, the model registry, the orders warehouse, the routing system and the carrier's delivery scans, which supply the labels. Each dependency is a contract with an owner, not an implementation detail.

A requirement only helps if it says what is measured, how it is measured, and against which target. The checkout predictor has five such contracts. Quality: a late-risk log loss no higher than nought point four, measured weekly on orders whose labels have matured. Latency: the ninety-ninth percentile at or under a hundred and fifty milliseconds, per request. Freshness: features no more than fifteen minutes old at request time. Availability: ninety-nine point nine percent over thirty days, which leaves an error budget of forty-three point two minutes of failure a month. And cost: no more than twenty pence per thousand calls. Now read one week of production observations, two thousand checkout requests. The median is thirty-eight milliseconds and the ninety-fifth percentile fifty-four, both comfortably inside the target. But the ninety-ninth percentile is a hundred and eighty-nine milliseconds, so the latency contract is broken. Thirty-two of the two thousand requests take more than a hundred and fifty milliseconds, a slow tail caused by cold reads from the feature store. An average latency would have hidden this entirely, which is why latency contracts are written against percentiles, and why each contract names its measurement as well as its target.

A modelling notebook usually does everything in one place: it loads data, builds features, trains, evaluates and scores, with state passed between cells. A production system needs those steps as components with stated inputs and outputs. Here the notebook becomes five. Load orders takes a named snapshot and returns a frame. Build features is a single pure function. Train and evaluate return a model and a report as explicit outputs, rather than leaving them in memory. And there are two scoring entry points: score batch for the nightly planning job, and predict for one checkout request. The most important choice is that training, the batch job and the online service all call the same build features function. If each has its own copy, the copies drift apart over time, and the model starts receiving different inputs in production from the ones it was trained on. Passing an as-of time into the function makes the time boundary part of its signature, so it is hard to use a column that would not have been known yet. Finally, the prediction type carries the model version that produced it. Every output in the system should say which model made it, or nothing downstream can be traced.

Turning modelling code into maintainable software means packaging it, pinning what it depends on, and testing the contracts between its components. Pinning matters more than usual, because the model was fitted with particular library versions, and a different version of a preprocessing library can change its outputs without any error. Settings such as feature lists and thresholds belong in a configuration file, not as literals buried in the code. Then the tests, and what each one can show. A unit test shows that a feature function meets its specification, for example that a distance is never negative. A schema test shows that requests are well formed, with all fourteen fields present and typed. A contract test shows that predict returns a risk between nought and one, along with a model version, so callers can rely on the shape. A smoke test shows the package installs, loads and returns one prediction. Some tests guard modelling assumptions directly, such as asserting that an outcome column like delivered at never appears among the features. But be clear about what a passing suite cannot show. It says nothing about whether the predictions are accurate, and nothing about business value. That needs model evaluation and experiments.

Every dependency fails sometimes, so the system's behaviour in each failure case should be decided in advance, written down, and visible in the response. For the checkout predictor, a malformed request is rejected with a four twenty-two error that names the failing field. If the feature store takes longer than forty milliseconds, the service answers with a simple rule-based delivery window instead of waiting and breaking the latency contract. If one feature is stale, the service still predicts, but flags which feature was old. If the model produces a value outside nought to one, something is badly wrong, so it falls back and raises an alert. And every fallback response says so explicitly, with its source set to fallback, so nothing downstream mistakes a rule for the model. Loading the model is its own boundary. The service checks the file's hash against the manifest before loading it, and if the check fails, it refuses to start. It stays unready, so the load balancer sends it no traffic, which is far better than serving an unverified model. It also avoids formats such as raw pickle, which can run arbitrary code when loaded, and checks that the model's expected input schema matches what it will receive.

More automation is not automatically better. Every tool added to an ML system is another system that has to be run, upgraded and understood, so the level of automation should match how the model is actually used. Four levels are a useful guide. Manual means a notebook run by hand, with the model file copied somewhere, which is fine for a one-off analysis and nothing more. Scripted means a package with tests, a scheduled job and versioned models, the minimum for any model someone depends on. A pipeline adds orchestrated retraining, validation gates and a model registry. A platform adds shared feature, serving and monitoring infrastructure used by many models and teams. Moving up a level is justified by a few questions. How often does the model change? What does a bad model break, and how quickly? Who owns it, and who is woken at three in the morning when it fails? And what will the new tool cost to keep running? For this retailer today, the checkout predictor sits in every checkout and retrains monthly, so it is moving from scripted to a pipeline. The daily planning job is one nightly job with one owner, and scripted is enough. The rest of the course builds these pieces only where they are justified.

A training dataset is only reproducible if its columns, units, keys and origin are written down and checked, rather than remembered by whoever built it. That written description is the dataset contract. Each column states a type and a unit. Distance is in kilometres, weight is in kilograms. Each has a rule, such as distance greater than nought and at most eighty kilometres, which covers every delivery zone. Each names its source and owner: the checkout API, the geo service, the warehouse, or the carrier's delivery scans. And the label, whether a delivery was late, is only set once it has matured. The dataset as a whole has three more properties. A key, one row per order identifier, so duplicates are detectable. A snapshot, here taken as of one o'clock on the first of March, with fifty-two thousand rows, so the same training set can be named and rebuilt. And provenance, including a hash of the query that produced it. Notice what a schema alone cannot catch. If a source starts sending distances in metres, every value is still a perfectly valid floating-point number. Only a range rule, or a comparison with past data, notices that a three-kilometre trip has become three thousand.

Rows that break the dataset contract should be held, not deleted and not silently accepted. The source fixes them, and the batch is replayed. Here is one day's batch of ten thousand incoming order rows. Forty-two have no delivery zone and seventeen have impossible weights, so they go to quarantine. Nine are duplicate order identifiers, which is common when a client retries, so the latest version is kept and the others logged. And a hundred and twenty have distances over eighty kilometres. They all come from one source, which has started sending metres instead of kilometres, the failure a schema check alone would have missed. Nine thousand eight hundred and twelve rows are accepted. Quarantine is better than dropping for two reasons. Dropped rows simply vanish, and if they share a cause, such as one region or one carrier, the bias they introduce is invisible. Quarantined rows are counted, so a rising quarantine rate can raise an alert. The raw batch itself stays append-only, so nothing is ever lost. When the source re-sends the corrected distances, the same rules run again over the replayed batch, and the result is a new snapshot with a new identity, rather than a quiet edit to the old one.

A label only exists once the outcome is known, and the orders that do not have one must be counted, explained and kept out of the split on purpose. At the first of March snapshot there are fifty-two thousand orders from January and February. The label, late or not, is set three days after the promised delivery date, which gives delayed scans time to arrive. Ninety-four point one percent of orders were delivered and have a label, forty-eight thousand nine hundred and thirty-two orders. Three point two percent were cancelled before dispatch, so there was no delivery to be late. Nought point four percent were lost in transit. They are excluded from training, but reported separately, because a lost parcel is arguably the worst kind of late. And two point three percent, the most recent orders, have not matured yet. Including them would label them all on time by default. The split manifest then pins the exact training, validation and test orders, split by checkout date with the test set the latest. It stores frozen lists of order identifiers with their hashes, rather than a query that could return different rows if re-run later. And it records the exclusion counts, so anyone can check what was left out, and why.

Every record in this system has more than one clock, and the difference between them is where many leaks come from. The event time is when something happened, here when a parcel was delivered. The ingestion time is when the record arrived in the data pipeline. And the availability time is when a feature computation could actually read it, which can be later still. A feature used at prediction time may only use what was available then, not merely what had already happened. Look at delivery zone N7 for a checkout at two in the afternoon. Most delivery scans stream in from the carrier about fifteen minutes after the delivery itself. But scan s5, a parcel delivered at thirteen thirty-five, arrived as part of a carrier batch upload at fourteen fifty, seventy-five minutes late. And scan s6, delivered at thirteen fifty, became readable at five past two. Both deliveries had happened before the checkout, yet neither was known to the live service when it made its prediction. The consequence is direct. A training set that filters only on event time gives the model information it will never have in production, and its offline evaluation will look better than anything it can achieve live.

The value of a feature in a training row must be the value the live service could have computed at that moment. The chapter's worked example shows four ways of computing one feature, the average delivery delay in an order's zone over the three hours before checkout. The live service, at two in the afternoon, could read scans s1 to s4, and scan s3 still showed its original delay of ninety-five minutes. The average was thirty-eight point seven five minutes, and that is what the model saw. A naive join on event time, run the next day, also picks up the late scans s5 and s6, plus a correction made to s3 at half past three, and gets forty-one point one seven. An as-of join that filters on availability, but reads from a table holding only the current, corrected values, gets twenty-one point two five, because s3 now reads twenty-five. Only an as-of join over the history of values reproduces thirty-eight point seven five. Two conditions make it correct: filtering on availability time, not just event time, and reading each value as it stood at that moment, which requires keeping every version with its validity window. The correction is real, but it was not known at two o'clock. All four results pass a schema check.

Even with one feature definition shared by both paths, the value served to the model online and the value recomputed offline for training can differ. The way to know by how much is to measure parity on logged requests. In this example the online feature store is materialised every fifteen minutes, so a checkout request reads the value from the last refresh, while the offline as-of join recomputes the feature at the exact request time. Across four hundred logged checkout requests, seventy-nine point eight percent agree within two minutes. Twenty-eight differ by more than ten minutes, almost all of them requests that arrived shortly after a burst of late deliveries in their zone, which the online store had not yet picked up. Parity depends on three things. One feature definition, used by both paths, so the code cannot drift. A refresh rate matched to how quickly the value actually changes. And logging the value that was actually served, with its timestamp, so the comparison can be made at all. It also raises a design choice. If production will keep reading values up to fifteen minutes old, training on the served values, lag included, matches what the model will see. Training on perfectly fresh values teaches it a precision it never gets.

Every feature will sometimes be missing or too old, so the policy has to be decided per feature, and it has to match what the model saw in training. For the zone delay feature, a value older than thirty minutes is replaced by the zone's weekly median, and an indicator flag is set. Two percent of training rows were imputed the same way, so the model has learned how much to trust that value. The customer late rate is missing for every new customer, so the model receives a missing indicator, again a case it saw many times in training. Distance is essential: without it the service refuses to predict and answers with the rule-based delivery window. The fourth row is the problem. A stale weather risk is replaced by zero, which the model reads as normal weather, and it never saw substituted values in training. That is a silent default. It looks like real data, nothing records that it happened, and on a stormy day it quietly removes the model's most useful signal. So there are four semantics: impute a training statistic, add an indicator the model learned, refuse openly, or the silent default, which should be avoided. Whichever is used, stale features are named in the response and in the logs.

A feature store gathers several of this chapter's responsibilities in one tool. It registers one definition per feature, runs point-in-time joins for training, materialises values into a low-latency online store, and records versions and owners. It is useful, but it has limits worth stating. It can store a definition, but cannot judge whether that definition is correct. It runs point-in-time joins, but only on the timestamps it is given, so if availability time was never recorded, it cannot know when data was really available. And it can materialise values, but cannot make a stale value fresh. Changing a feature shows why evolution has to be explicit. Suppose the zone delay should become a three-hour median instead of a mean, to resist outliers. The change is made under a new name, version two, and version one is left untouched. Version two's history is backfilled, so the next training run can use as-of values. A new model version is trained and validated on it. The old and new features are served side by side, so the current model keeps working and rollback remains possible. Version one is retired only once it has been checked that no model still reads it. The rule is simple: a new meaning gets a new name, and a unit is never changed in place.

A training run is defined by everything that could change its result, and each of those things should be recorded as an identity, something that names one exact version, rather than as a description. There are five, plus the split. The code is identified by a git commit, together with a flag saying whether the working tree had uncommitted changes, because a dirty tree means the commit does not describe what ran. The data is a named snapshot, such as the orders snapshot version three as of the first of March, never just the orders table, which changes every day. The features are a feature view and its version. The configuration is the file, its hash and the random seed. The environment is the container image digest and the dependency lock file, since library versions can change results. And the split is its manifest and a fingerprint of its identifiers. The run manifest on the left records all of them in a few lines. The cost of missing one is concrete. Without the commit, or with a dirty tree, nobody knows what code ran. Without the snapshot identifier, nobody knows which rows were used. And without the image digest, the library versions that produced the model are lost.

An experiment tracker records each run's parameters, metrics and artefacts, so runs can be compared later. Fingerprints decide which of those runs can be compared at all. Take three runs, all validation evidence. Run A, the baseline gradient-boosted model, scores a log loss of nought point three nine four one, on a split whose fingerprint is c f 1 d 8 1 d 1. Run B adds a weather risk feature and is evaluated on the same split, with the same fingerprint, scoring nought point three nine nought two, a fair improvement. Run C makes the same change and scores better still, nought point three eight one five. But its split fingerprint is different. Its validation set differs from A's by a single order identifier, enough to make the comparison invalid, and a difference that would be invisible without the fingerprint. So log every parameter, not only the ones being tuned, because a default that changes between library versions is still a parameter. Log metrics per split, and per step when training curves matter. Log the artefacts: the model, its evaluation report and its plots. And tag every run with the data and split fingerprints. A fingerprint is a hash of the split's identifier list, so any change at all produces a new value.

Lineage links each artefact to what produced it: this model came from this run, which used this feature view, built from this snapshot. It tells you exactly what ran. What it cannot do is bring back inputs that no longer exist, or force a rerun to produce identical output. Try re-running model version twelve from its record six months later. The snapshot path is recorded, but the snapshot itself was deleted by the retention policy, so the training data cannot be rebuilt. The container image was kept, so at least the library versions match. Feature view version five still exists by name, but its source table has since been rewritten, so the same name now gives different values. The seed, seventeen, was logged, yet multithreaded training still adds floating-point numbers in a varying order. And the rerun scores nought point three nine two four against the recorded nought point three nine four one: close, but not the same. So be precise about which promise is being made. Traceable means we know what ran. Re-runnable means every input still exists, which requires retention policies to protect the inputs of any model still in use. Deterministic means bit-identical output, which is rarely promised, and should never be assumed from a logged seed.

A training job is easier to trust when it is treated as a contract: it reads named inputs, writes its outputs somewhere private, and publishes them in one final step. Anything looser can leave half a model where something else will find it. The inputs are the snapshot, the split manifest and the configuration, all read-only, and all named by identity, so a rerun reads exactly the same things. The outputs are written first to a staging path that no other system reads. Before publishing, the job checks itself: every expected file is present, the model's input schema matches the feature view, and the checksums are correct. Then it publishes the whole set to the candidates location with a single atomic step, such as a rename, so a reader sees either nothing or everything. Only after that does it exit successfully, so the orchestrator never records success for a job whose outputs are not there. What gets published together matters too: the model, its input signature, its evaluation report, its run manifest and a checksum file. A candidate without its report or signature is incomplete, and should never be published, because every later step, validation, registration and serving, depends on all of them arriving together.

Every training job costs time and compute, so estimate the cost before running it, and give hyperparameter tuning a fixed budget that is declared in advance and the same for every candidate. The estimate here is simple. One trial of the gradient-boosted model takes about six minutes on eight CPUs with sixteen gigabytes of memory. Forty trials are therefore four CPU-hours, and on four parallel workers about one hour of wall time. Ten trials would take a fifth of an hour. The budget is a choice to make deliberately, not something to discover afterwards. The plot shows what this search actually found, as validation evidence. The best log loss, nought point three nine four one, appeared at trial six. The remaining thirty-four trials found nothing better, so in hindsight most of the budget bought confirmation rather than improvement. There is a subtler point too: the best of many trials is optimistic, because it was selected using the very validation set it is scored on, so its true performance is likely a little worse. On the scheduling side, giving every trial the same fixed resources lets trials share one queue. And a declared budget is what makes comparisons between candidates fair: a model tuned for ten times longer has not proved a better design.

Long training jobs on cheap, interruptible machines will sometimes be stopped part-way, so a checkpoint must hold all of the state needed to continue as though nothing had happened. Here is one interrupted job. It trains a thousand boosting rounds at about two point four seconds each, saving a checkpoint every hundred rounds. The checkpoint at round seven hundred is written at nine forty-three. At round seven hundred and thirty, the spot instance is reclaimed, and the job dies. The orchestrator's retry finds the latest checkpoint and resumes from round seven hundred, so only thirty rounds, about a minute of work, are repeated. Round one thousand finishes at ten o'clock, and only then is the model evaluated and published. A checkpoint that holds only the model so far is not enough. It must also hold the random number generator's state, so that row and column sampling continue the same sequence, and the position in the data, so no batch is skipped or seen twice. Without those, the resumed model differs from one that ran uninterrupted, with no error to show it. And the checkpoint itself is written to a temporary file and then renamed, so a crash mid-write cannot corrupt it. The partial model left in staging by the interruption is never published.

A retry only helps when the failure might not happen again, so the retry policy should depend on the kind of failure. A spot preemption, or a temporary five-oh-three error from the object store, is transient: retry, with backoff, from the latest checkpoint, up to a small limit. Running out of memory is a resource problem. Retrying on the same machine fails the same way, so fail, and resize once, deliberately. A failed schema check or a loss that becomes not-a-number is deterministic. A retry will produce exactly the same failure, so fail immediately, and keep the logs and the last checkpoint for diagnosis, rather than burning three retries' worth of compute. Even a successful run varies. Five reruns of the same configuration, with the same seed, on eight threads, give validation log losses from nought point three nine two two to nought point three nine two eight, a spread of about five ten-thousandths, because parallel floating-point sums are not added in a fixed order. A candidate that beats the current model by less than that is indistinguishable from noise. So declare a tolerance before comparing candidates, not after seeing the numbers, and for close calls compare across several seeds rather than a single run each.

A pipeline is a directed graph of components. Each component declares its inputs and outputs with types, and the edges of the graph are the artefacts passed between them. Here is the retraining pipeline for the late-risk model, version four. Take snapshot produces a dataset. Validate data checks that dataset against the contract from chapter two, and produces a report. Build features runs only after the check passes, which is an explicit dependency in the graph, not an assumption about timing. Train turns the feature table into a model, and evaluate scores the model on the split, producing metrics. Typing each component buys several things. A component reads only its declared inputs and writes only its declared output, so the orchestrator can see every dependency, and knows which steps can run in parallel and which must wait. Each component runs in a container image pinned by digest, the same environment identity recorded for training runs in chapter three. And the artefact is the interface. Components never share memory or a working directory, so any one of them can be rerun, replaced or tested in isolation. The code card shows the same graph declared in a pipeline language, with each step wired to the outputs of the steps it depends on.

Gates turn a straight pipeline into branches. A run can end as a candidate model, or it can stop early for a stated reason, and both are normal outcomes of a healthy pipeline. This pipeline has two gates. The data gate asks whether the new snapshot meets its contract. The evaluation gate asks whether a newly trained model beats the current champion by a declared margin. Between the two, a gradient-boosted model and a logistic regression train in parallel, since neither depends on the other. Three monthly runs show the branches in use. In January both gates pass. The gradient-boosted model scores a validation log loss of nought point three nine four one, against the champion's nought point three nine nine, so the run ends with a candidate for release review. In February, one point two percent of distances arrive in metres, the source error from chapter two, so the run stops at the data gate and alerts the data owner, before any compute is spent on training. In March both models train, but the best scores nought point three nine five one against the new champion's nought point three nine four one, so there is no gain and the champion stays. None of these is a failure. Each stop names its reason and its owner.

A pipeline run can be started by a schedule, by a data event such as a new snapshot being published, or by a person. Its identity, though, should come from what it computes, not from whatever started it. The run key here combines the pipeline version with its parameters, giving something like retrain, version four, first of April, plus a short hash. The table shows why that matters. At three o'clock on the first of April the monthly schedule fires. At four minutes past, the snapshot-published event fires for the same snapshot. Both resolve to the same pipeline version and the same snapshot date, so they produce the same run key, and the second is deduplicated instead of running the whole pipeline twice. A manual rerun of March gets a different key, because its snapshot date differs, and so does a run of pipeline version five, because the code changed. The parameters themselves must come from the data interval being processed, never from the current clock. A step that asks for today's date computes something different every time it is rerun, so a rerun next week would no longer mean the same run. Finally, the orchestrator allows one active run per key, and skips a trigger for a key that is already running.

Orchestrators cache steps to avoid repeating work. A step's cache key is a hash of its code and its declared inputs, and if the key has been seen before, the stored output is reused. A cache hit is therefore only as good as its key, because anything a step reads without declaring it is invisible to the cache. Here the April pipeline is rerun after a fix to the zone lookup table, which maps postcodes to delivery zones. Every step's code is unchanged and every declared input is unchanged, so every step is a cache hit. But build features also reads the zone lookup table, and never declared it as an input. Its cached output was computed with the old zones and is now stale, and so are the model trained from it and the metrics computed from that model. The rerun reports success within seconds, and changes nothing at all. There are three common kinds of undeclared input to look for: a latest table that is updated in place, the current time read from the clock, and an unpinned library in the environment. The fix is to declare the zone lookup table, at a specific version, as an input of build features. Then a new version of the table changes the cache key, and the step reruns.

Orchestrators guarantee that a step runs at least once, not exactly once. A step that writes outside the pipeline must therefore be safe to run twice, because sometimes it will be. Here is the daily planning job's publish step, which writes tomorrow's predicted delivery durations into a table owned by the routing system. At three forty-four, an insert of a hundred and eighty thousand rows commits successfully. But the step times out before it can report success back to the orchestrator. From the orchestrator's point of view the step failed, so at three forty-six it retries, and an append-style insert writes all hundred and eighty thousand rows again. At ten past four, routing plans drivers from three hundred and sixty thousand rows, with every order appearing twice. The fix is to make the write idempotent, so that running it twice has the same effect as running it once. Give each row an idempotency key, here the plan date and the order identifier, and use a merge on that key. The retry then updates the same rows, and the table still holds a hundred and eighty thousand. Alternatively, write to a staging table and swap it in with a single commit. Either way, the workflow engine cannot undo an external write for you; the step itself must allow for being repeated.

A backfill reruns a pipeline over past partitions, usually because something upstream was fixed. Here the zone lookup fix means thirty nights of planning scores should be recomputed. Planning it starts with arithmetic. Each night takes about forty minutes on four CPUs. The team's quota is sixteen CPUs, so at most four nights can run at once. Run one at a time, the backfill would take twenty hours and overlap with the normal nightly run. Run four in parallel, it takes about five and a third hours, eight rounds of forty minutes, and still leaves room for tonight's run. Priorities matter as much as parallelism. The regular nightly run has priority over the backfill, so tonight's scores still land by five in the morning, while the backfill runs in a separate low-priority pool and waits when capacity is needed. And each backfilled night records the same run key a normal run for that night would have, so it can be found and compared, plus the reason for the backfill, the pipeline and feature versions it used, and the run key of the output it replaces. Without that record, nobody can later tell an original night from a recomputed one, or work out which model saw which version of the data.

The same pipeline definition can usually run both locally, on a developer's laptop, and remotely, on the shared orchestrator. That portability is valuable, but it does not make the two environments the same. Locally, steps run as processes, against a small sample of the data in local files, using the developer's own credentials and whatever resources the laptop has, with metadata kept in a local store. Remotely, steps run as containers on a cluster, against the full snapshot in the object store, each with its own service identity and declared resources, recording shared metadata with lineage. So each place catches different failures. Local runs are good at catching logic errors, shape mismatches and schema problems, quickly. Remote runs reveal memory limits, timeouts and permission errors, which only appear at full scale or under a real identity. Portability covers the definition itself: the same graph, the same parameters, and the same digest-pinned images. It does not cover scale, because a one percent sample hides the memory a full run needs. And it does not cover permissions, because a developer's broad credentials hide grants that the pipeline's service identity is missing. Treat a local run as a fast first check, not as evidence that the remote run will succeed.

Before a candidate model can be released, it is checked in three layers, and those layers answer different questions and produce different kinds of result. The software layer asks whether the code runs correctly. Does predict return a risk between nought and one? Does the bundle load in the serving image? The data layer asks whether the inputs are valid: does the protected test set meet the dataset contract? Both of these give a pass or a fail, and running them again gives the same answer. The model layer asks whether the candidate is good enough: its log loss compared with the current champion, or its recall of late deliveries in rural zones. These results are estimates. Computed on a different sample of orders, they would give a slightly different number, so each one is an estimate with an interval around it, not a yes or no. A release gate therefore needs both kinds of rule. Deterministic checks are simple: any failure blocks the release. Statistical checks need more care. They need a declared margin, the improvement that would actually matter, and they have to be read against the uncertainty in the estimate. The next sections build both, using the late-risk candidate, version thirteen.

A candidate is compared with the model that is serving now, the champion, on a protected test set that is used for nothing else. The comparison needs an estimate of uncertainty, not just two numbers. The protected set here is two thousand four hundred matured orders, never used to train, tune or select any model. As a floor, a simple zone-average baseline scores a log loss of nought point four four one. The champion, version twelve, scores nought point three nine seven four, and the candidate, version thirteen, nought point three nine three six. The paired difference is minus nought point nought nought three eight. How sure can we be that this is a real improvement? Resampling the two thousand four hundred per-order differences a thousand times, with replacement, gives the distribution in the plot, and a ninety-five percent interval from minus nought point nought nought five three to minus nought point nought nought two three. The whole interval lies beyond the declared margin of minus nought point nought nought two, so on overall log loss the candidate passes. The comparison is paired, which matters. Both models are scored on exactly the same orders, so how hard each order is cancels out, leaving a much tighter interval than comparing two separate averages would.

Version thirteen wins on overall log loss, but better on average is not enough. The release review checks what the average hides, and what the serving contract requires. Overall log loss improves by nought point nought nought three eight, a pass. But late-delivery recall in rural zones falls to nought point six six, below the declared floor of nought point seven, a fail. Rural orders are a minority, so the average improved while one group of customers got worse. Calibration error is nought point nought one nine, under the limit of nought point nought three, which matters because the predicted risk itself sets the delivery window shown at checkout. On orders from new customers, a robustness check for people the model has not seen before, log loss is within the allowed tolerance, so that passes. Then the resource checks, from a load test at forty requests a second. The candidate's ninety-ninth percentile latency is a hundred and eighty-two milliseconds, against a limit of a hundred and fifty, because it is a much larger ensemble. That is a fail. The champion, after the feature-cache fix from chapter one, runs at a hundred and twenty-one. Memory is seven hundred and sixty megabytes, under the limit. A more accurate model that breaks the latency contract is simply not deployable.

A gate policy turns the evidence into a verdict, and it must be written before anyone sees the results, or the thresholds drift towards whatever the candidate achieved. This policy has two parts. First, hard criteria: ninety-ninth percentile latency, rural recall and calibration. Any failure blocks the release, however good the rest looks. Second, a quality rule on the bootstrap interval of the log-loss difference. The candidate passes if the whole ninety-five percent interval is at or below minus nought point nought nought two. It fails if the whole interval shows it to be worse than the champion. Anything else is inconclusive. Version thirteen passes the quality rule, but fails two hard criteria, so the verdict is fail, with the reasons recorded. A lighter variant, thirteen lite, was built to meet the latency limit, and passes every hard criterion. But its interval runs from minus nought point nought nought one eight to plus nought point nought nought one, so it might be slightly better than the champion, or slightly worse. That is inconclusive. Inconclusive is a real answer, not a soft pass. It leads to more data, such as waiting for another month of matured labels, or to a controlled online test, and the champion keeps serving meanwhile.

A model file on its own cannot reproduce the scores it was validated with. What gets released is a bundle, holding everything the serving runtime needs to compute exactly what was evaluated. Inside the bundle is the fitted model, and alongside it the preprocessing it was trained with, the category encoders, imputers and scalers, because a model fed differently encoded inputs produces different predictions with no error at all. There is a signature, listing every input field with its type and unit, and every output, so the server can validate each request before predicting, and callers know that late risk will lie between nought and one. There is the feature version the model was trained on, checkout features version five, so the runtime reads the right features. There are the exact library versions, because some formats cannot be loaded across versions and some numerical results drift. There is the evaluation report, the evidence it passed its gates, which an audit or a later rollback will need. And there is a hash of every file, so integrity can be checked before anything is loaded. Each missing piece fails in its own way, and the worst ones fail silently. Without the preprocessing, inputs change without any error.

When a model is promoted, three different things happen, and they happen at different times. Confusing them is a common source of incidents. At ten o'clock, version fourteen is registered. That creates a new, immutable version in the registry, but nothing serves it yet. At ten thirty, the champion alias is moved to point at version fourteen. The registry has now changed, but the serving pods are still running version twelve, because they only load a new model when they next check the alias. From ten thirty-one they start reloading, and by ten thirty-six all six pods serve version fourteen. Rollback has the same lag. At ten past eleven the alias is moved back to version twelve, yet the pods keep serving version fourteen until they reload again. So keep three states apart. A version is immutable: version fourteen always means exactly one bundle. An alias is a mutable pointer, which says what should be serving. The runtime is what is actually loaded, right now, in each pod. The registry can only tell you the first two. The only proof of what is live is the model version that every response carries, which is why the prediction contract in chapter one included it.

Loading a model file can run code. A pickle or joblib file can execute arbitrary Python as it is loaded, so loading one from an untrusted source is equivalent to running a stranger's program on the serving machine. Formats should therefore be chosen by what loading them can do. Pickle and joblib can do anything, so they should only ever come from your own trusted, verified builds. Skops loads only types on an allowed list, and asks for review of any unknown type. ONNX is a graph of known operators, so loading it runs no arbitrary code, though it ties you to an operator-set version. Plain JSON trees and text formats are data only, and need only a schema check. The environment matters as well. The bundle records the library versions it was built with. Serving with the same scikit-learn version is fine. Serving with an older version should be refused, because the file may depend on newer internals. And a gradient-boosting library whose tree format changed between versions should be refused too, rather than loaded and trusted. The check belongs at startup, before anything is loaded. Compare the bundle's lock file with the runtime's installed versions, and fail with a clear message, rather than failing later, or worse, not failing at all.

Every release leaves evidence that someone will need later, for an audit, for an incident investigation, or for a rollback. So decide in advance what is kept, for how long, and who owns it. For each released version, the bundle and its hashes are kept while the version is live and for a year afterwards. The gate report and its verdict are kept for two years, as is the approval record that says who released it. The split manifest and test identifiers are kept so the evaluation can be checked. And the training snapshot is kept for as long as any model built on it is still live, which is exactly the retention gap that made the rerun in chapter three impossible. A rollback bundle needs more than the old model file. It needs version twelve's complete bundle, intact. It needs feature view version five to still be served, because if that view was retired when version fourteen moved to view six, the old model has no inputs to read. And it needs the configuration and thresholds that version twelve was used with. The last requirement is that the rollback is proven, not assumed. Restore the previous bundle in staging and confirm it loads and answers, before the day it is actually needed.

In an ML system, the phrase CI CD covers four separate automated loops, each with its own trigger, its own output, and things it must not do. Continuous integration is triggered by a code change. It runs the tests and builds the serving image, once, producing a tested artefact. Continuous training is triggered by new data or a schedule, the retraining pipeline from chapter four, and produces a candidate model together with its evidence. Continuous delivery takes a candidate that passed its gates and turns it into a release: a specific bundle with a specific image, ready to deploy. And deployment takes an approved release and actually moves traffic onto it. Keeping them separate matters. Continuous training produces candidates, but must not deploy them automatically: a model that passes its offline gates still needs a controlled rollout. A code change rebuilds the image, but does not retrain the model, so a refactor cannot silently change predictions. And deployment changes what is serving, but does not, on its own, prove that the new model helps the product. Each loop can then fail, be paused or roll back on its own. A broken training run does not block a security patch, and a security patch does not slip a new model into production.

The image that reaches production should be byte for byte the image that was tested. The way to guarantee that is to build it once, and then promote that exact artefact, by its digest, through each environment. Compare two ways of shipping the server for version fourteen. Built once, the image with digest nine one c nought is created and tested in CI, then the same digest runs in staging and the same digest runs in production. Rebuilt per environment, the CI image is fine, but the staging build resolves its dependencies on a different day and picks up a newer pandas release, and the production build a day later picks up another. Production now runs an image that nobody has tested. Everything that defines a release should be in version control. That includes the pipeline definitions themselves, the CI configuration and the retraining pipeline. It includes the infrastructure: the number of replicas, resource limits and autoscaling. And it includes the configuration, which should be small, and should differ between environments only where it must, such as endpoints and credentials. Promotion then becomes a recorded step that names the image digest and the model version. The production step also requires the staging checks to have passed, and an approval.

Development, staging and production should differ in three ways: the data they hold, the credentials they use, and who is allowed to deploy to them. Development uses synthetic data or a small sample. Staging uses a masked copy of production data, so realistic volumes and distributions without raw personal details. Production uses real orders. Each environment has its own service identity, and no credential is shared between them, so a mistake in staging cannot write to production. Anyone can deploy to development, only CI deploys to staging, and only continuous delivery deploys to production, after an approval. Moving a release up a level then needs stated evidence. From development to staging: the tests pass, the image is built, and the bundle's signature is valid. From staging to production: the bundle loads and answers against the staging feature store, a load test shows a ninety-ninth percentile latency within a hundred and fifty milliseconds, and the gate verdict from chapter five is pass. And from a canary to full traffic: the guardrails held for the whole canary window. Throughout, the same artefact moves all the way up, so the evidence gathered at each level applies to exactly what runs at the next one.

Rollout patterns differ in who sees the new version first, and in what evidence you get before everyone does. Blue-green deployment runs the new version alongside the old one and switches all traffic at once. Switching back is quick, but nobody is exposed to the new version before everyone is, so it supplies no live evidence in advance. A rolling deployment replaces pods one by one. It needs no extra capacity, but for a while some requests go to the old version and some to the new, and the evidence is hard to read. A canary sends a small share of traffic, here five percent of customers, to the new version first, watches it, and only then expands. It supplies live errors, latency and early effects, while limiting exposure to that five percent. Shadow deployment sends a copy of live requests to the new model, records its scores, and never uses them in a response. It shows live latency and how the scores differ, with nobody exposed at all, at the cost of double compute. But a shadow model never acts, so it supplies no evidence about outcomes. For the checkout predictor, a sensible sequence is shadow first, to check latency under real traffic, and then a canary assigned by customer.

A canary should be assigned by a stable unit, and its abort conditions should be decided before it starts. Here the unit is the customer. Each customer identifier is hashed together with a salt for this rollout, and the result taken modulo a hundred. Customers in buckets nought to four get version fourteen. Across twenty thousand customers that gives four point nine percent, close to the intended five, and because the hash never changes, a customer stays in the same arm for every checkout during the canary. Assigning by request instead, with a five percent coin flip each time, would put twenty-six percent of customers with six checkouts into both arms. The customer is the right unit because one customer should see one delivery-window policy. Seeing a narrow window on Monday and a wide one on Tuesday is confusing for them, and mixed exposure makes any later comparison between the arms hard to interpret. Then the guardrails, checked every five minutes on the canary arm. Abort if the error rate exceeds half a percent, or the ninety-ninth percentile latency exceeds a hundred and fifty milliseconds, for ten minutes. Abort if the fallback rate is more than twice the stable arm's. And abort if the mean predicted risk shifts by more than nought point nought five.

Late-delivery labels arrive days after checkout, because the delivery has to happen, and the label is only final three days after the promised date. A canary that ends after two days has therefore seen almost none of its own outcomes. For canary orders, the plot shows the share with a matured label by day after checkout. By day two it is zero. By day four it is thirty-four percent, and by day seven it is complete. So a forty-eight-hour canary gathers operational evidence only. It is worth being exact about which claims each kind of evidence supports, and when. That version fourteen runs safely is shown by errors, latency and fallback rates, within hours. That it scores live traffic the way it scored offline data is shown by comparing live and offline score distributions, from the first day. That it predicts better on live traffic needs log loss on matured labels, which exists only from about day seven. And that it improves the product, fewer broken delivery promises, needs a randomised comparison on the objective itself, which is an experiment, covered in chapter nine. Shadow deployments are the extreme case. A shadow model never acts, so however good its scores look, they show nothing about the outcomes its actions would have caused.

Rolling back a model is more than putting the old weights back. It only works if everything the old model depends on still exists, and still means the same thing. Take a rollback from version fourteen to version twelve. Version twelve's bundle was retained, as chapter five required, so that part is fine. Version twelve reads checkout features version five, which is still materialised alongside version six, so that is fine too. It reads the original zone delay mean, which is fine only if that feature was not retired when version fourteen moved to the median. Version fourteen added a basket value field to requests. Version twelve simply ignores the extra field, so that is fine. And version twelve was used with a risk threshold of nought point three, not version fourteen's nought point three five, so the configuration must roll back together with the model, or the old model runs with the new threshold. So a rollback should be done as one unit. Check the dependencies first. Move the alias together with its configuration. Then verify the runtime, by checking that responses now carry model version twelve. And be clear about what a rollback cannot undo: the delivery windows already shown to customers by version fourteen stay shown.

Every release should leave one record that answers the questions someone will ask later: what was released, on what evidence, approved by whom, how it rolled out, and how to undo it. The record for version fourteen names the model version and the image digest together, since either alone is ambiguous. It links the gate report and its verdict. It records who approved the release, and when. It holds the rollout plan, a five percent canary by customer for forty-eight hours, and the abort criteria, which were fixed before the rollout started, not adjusted once the numbers came in. It names the rollback target as a unit: model version twelve, with feature view five and configuration forty-one. And it lists each rollout event as it happened, here the canary starting, and two days later the expansion to all traffic with every guardrail held. Eventually the old version is retired, deliberately. After thirty stable days, the rollback alias is removed. Feature view five stops being materialised, but only once it has been checked that no live model reads it. The bundle is archived for the retention period set in chapter five. And the record is closed, saying when the version was retired and by whom. That closes the delivery loop for this release.

The daily planning job scores tomorrow's orders in one batch, read from a single snapshot, and split into partitions so the work can run in parallel and can fail in pieces rather than all at once. Tonight there are a hundred and eighty thousand orders, read from the one o'clock snapshot and split into sixty-four partitions by delivery zone. The zones are uneven. Four large city zones dominate, and the biggest holds ten thousand six hundred and fifty orders. At about eleven hundred orders a minute per worker, that partition alone takes nine and a half minutes. With four workers, assigning the longest partitions first, the whole night takes forty minutes, consistent with the backfill arithmetic in chapter four. There are three reasons for these choices. Every partition reads the same snapshot, so all of tonight's scores describe the same moment, rather than a mixture of states as orders change during the run. The partitions follow delivery zones, because that is how routing reads the output. And a failure only needs one partition retried, not the whole night. The run writes a manifest: its run key, the model version, the input snapshot, the number of rows it expects to produce, and the status of every partition, so a reader can tell a complete night from a partial one.

Every output row needs an identity, and the whole night of scores should become visible to readers in one step. Whether that is actually possible depends on the storage being written to. Each row carries a key, the plan date and the order identifier. It also carries the run key of the night that produced it, and the model version. Visibility then depends on the storage. A warehouse table can publish a night in one transaction, or by overwriting one partition atomically, so a reader sees either the old night or the new one, never both. Table formats such as Delta or Iceberg commit a whole set of files with a single entry in their log, which gives the same guarantee. A plain folder in an object store has no such step. Files appear one by one, so a reader that lists the folder mid-publish sees part of a night and may treat it as complete. The usual workaround is to write all the files first, and then swap a small pointer file naming the latest complete night, which only works if every reader follows the pointer. Duplicates need their own handling. The same order appearing in two partitions is caught by a uniqueness check before publishing, and a retried write is made safe by merging on the row key.

Partitions fail on their own, and what happens next should be decided by the downstream contract, not by whatever seems convenient at three in the morning. On the night of the third of April, sixty-one of the sixty-four partitions finished by two forty, ninety-six point two percent of orders. Zones seventeen, forty-two and fifty-eight failed, all with the same feature-store timeout. Because the work is partitioned, only those three are retried, six thousand nine hundred and twenty-eight orders, rather than the whole night. By two fifty-two all sixty-four partitions are done, the checks pass, and a minute later the night is published, comfortably before the deadline. The contract with routing is explicit. Scores must be published by five o'clock. A night is complete only with all sixty-four zones, so it is all or nothing. If the deadline is missed, routing uses yesterday's plan plus simple rules, and says that it did. And the scores are built from the one o'clock snapshot, which is their freshness. So if the retry had failed as well, the right action would be to hold the whole night, as the contract says, let routing use its fallback, and backfill the three zones afterwards. Publishing sixty-one zones would be an option only if routing's contract allowed partial nights.

A serving pod should only receive traffic once it can answer well, and the platform finds that out through two different questions, liveness and readiness. Follow a new pod for the checkout predictor. At nought seconds the container starts. At one second it compares the installed libraries with the bundle's lock file. From two seconds it verifies the file hashes and loads the model, which takes about eight seconds. From ten seconds it warms its feature cache for the two hundred busiest zones, to avoid the cold-read tail from chapter one. At fourteen seconds it runs a self-test, twenty known requests whose answers must match, and only then reports ready and starts receiving traffic. Liveness asks whether the process is stuck. If the liveness endpoint stops answering, the platform restarts the pod. Readiness asks whether the pod can answer well right now. If not, the platform stops sending it requests, but leaves it running. The difference matters later in the pod's life. If the feature store becomes unreachable, the pod is still alive, so restarting it would only add a cold start, but it is not ready. It is taken out of rotation until the store returns. Meanwhile, every request it does receive is validated against the bundle's signature.

The latency contract from chapter one covers the whole path of a request, not just the model, so each step needs a ninety-ninth percentile allocation, and the allocations need to leave room for queueing. One checkout request goes in order: the checkout API calls the predictor, the request is validated against the signature, the online features for the order's zone and customer are fetched, the model predicts in-process, the prediction is logged, and the response returns to checkout, which shows the delivery window. The allocations are: twelve milliseconds for the network in, including TLS. Three for parsing and validation. Forty for the feature fetch, which is enforced as a timeout rather than merely hoped for. Twenty-five for the model's prediction. Five for post-processing and logging, and ten for the network out. Those add up to ninety-five milliseconds, leaving fifty-five for queueing and the unpredictable tail. Two lessons usually hold. The feature fetch, a network call to another system, dominates the tail far more often than the model does, which is why it has a hard deadline and a fallback. And log writes happen asynchronously, never on the request path, so a slow logging system cannot slow down checkout.

Waiting time in a serving system does not grow steadily with load. It stays nearly flat, and then climbs steeply as a replica approaches its capacity. That shape is the most important thing to know about overload. One replica of the checkout predictor has four workers, and each request takes about thirty milliseconds of work, so its capacity is about a hundred and thirty-three requests a second. A simple queueing model gives the mean time a request spends in the system as the service time divided by one minus the utilisation. At forty requests a second, the retailer's peak, that is forty-three milliseconds. At a hundred requests a second it is a hundred and twenty. At a hundred and twenty requests a second it is three hundred milliseconds, twice the contract, even though the replica is still below its theoretical capacity. So the policies aim to stay to the left of the knee. Keep the queue bounded, so that excess requests are rejected quickly instead of waiting forever. Shed load above seventy percent utilisation with a too-many-requests response, which checkout turns into the fallback window. Autoscale on load, targeting around fifty percent utilisation. Micro-batching, grouping requests into one model call, helps models on GPUs, but this CPU model gains nothing from it.

The same failure, a feature-store timeout, calls for opposite responses in the nightly job and in a checkout request, because their time budgets are completely different. In the nightly job there are hours until the five o'clock deadline, and nobody is waiting for an individual answer. So the right response is to retry the failed partition, up to twice, and drop its staging output if it is finally given up. In a checkout request, the customer is waiting, and the feature fetch has already used its forty millisecond deadline. There is no time for a retry. Instead, the request cancels the feature call when its deadline passes, so the work does not continue uselessly in the background, computes the rule-based delivery window from the distance and zone two milliseconds later, and responds at forty-seven milliseconds, well within the contract. That answer is a fallback, and three rules apply to it. It is documented: what it computes, and from which inputs. It is labelled, with the source set to fallback and no model version, so nothing downstream, from the logs to a monitoring dashboard to an analysis of model quality, mistakes it for the model's prediction. And it is counted, with its own rate and alert, because a rising fallback rate is a failure in progress.

Caching can remove a lot of latency, but a cache is only safe if its key includes everything that changes the answer. Zone features can be cached for sixty seconds, keyed by zone and by feature version, so that rolling out a new feature version can never serve old cached values. Customer features change slowly and can be cached for ten minutes. A whole prediction can rarely be cached, because its key would have to include every input and the model version, and inputs such as the zone's recent delays change constantly. The model itself is cached in memory in each pod, keyed by the bundle hash. Every response then attributes itself. It carries the model version and the feature version that produced it, its source, model or fallback, any features that were stale, and a request identifier that joins it to the logs. That attribution is what makes the monitoring in the next chapter possible, and it is the only reliable record of what was actually served. Finally, placement. A gradient-boosted model that predicts in twenty-five milliseconds on a CPU gains nothing from a GPU, so it runs on CPU pods. And it runs in the same region as the online feature store, because the feature fetch is the largest share of the latency budget.

Observability starts with deciding what matters to users and how much failure is acceptable. A service level indicator, or SLI, measures something users actually feel. For the checkout predictor it is the share of requests answered well, meaning successfully and within a hundred and fifty milliseconds. A service level objective, or SLO, sets a target for that indicator over a window, here ninety-nine point nine percent over thirty days. Whatever the target allows to fail is the error budget. At an average of twelve requests a second, April has thirty-one million one hundred and four thousand requests, so the budget is thirty-one thousand one hundred and four bad ones. The plot shows how April spent it, all production observation. On day six, a nine-minute feature-store failover cost sixteen thousand two hundred bad requests, fifty-two percent of the budget in one go. On day fourteen, a bad configuration push cost nine thousand six hundred, another thirty-one percent. On day twenty-three, draining a node pool degraded a fifth of requests for twenty-two minutes, ten percent more. By day twenty-three, ninety-three percent is gone. The budget then guides decisions. While budget remains, the team can ship changes. Once it is spent, risky changes wait until reliability is restored, and each SLO has a named owning team.

Each system needs a small set of operational signals, and each signal should alert on a condition it is there to catch. Online and batch systems need different ones. For the checkout predictor, ninety-ninth percentile latency and the error rate catch slow features, overload and bad deployments. Saturation, CPU above seventy percent or a queue longer than twenty, warns before the replica reaches the knee of its latency curve from chapter seven. The fallback rate, alerting above two percent for fifteen minutes, catches a dependency that is failing quietly, while the service itself looks healthy. And feature age catches a stuck materialisation job, when the zone delay feature has not been refreshed for over thirty minutes. The daily planning job has no latency in this sense. Its signals are whether the night is published by half past four, giving half an hour before the deadline. Whether the number of rows published is within two percent of the number expected, which catches missing zones and duplicates. And whether the input snapshot is more than twenty-six hours old, which would mean the job has scored yesterday's data again. What none of these signals can see is a service that is fast, valid and wrong. That needs the data and quality monitoring later in this chapter.

Logs, metrics and traces answer different questions, and all three must carry the identity of the model and the data, or diagnosis stalls at the first step. The prediction log records one event per request, with every input and output, so a single prediction can be reconstructed or replayed. Metrics are counts, latencies and rates, cheap to store and aggregate, and they drive dashboards and alerts. Traces follow one request across services, as spans, showing for example that the feature fetch took twenty-one of a request's forty-seven milliseconds. Look at one prediction event. It has a request identifier and a timestamp. It carries the customer as a keyed hash, not the raw identifier. It names the model version and the feature version. It records the feature values actually used, which stale features there were, and whether the answer came from the model or a fallback, followed by the risk, the window shown, and the latency split. Metric labels need a different discipline. Model version, source and zone have only a few values each, so they can be labels, letting every metric be broken down by model version during a canary. Order identifiers have millions of values, and as labels they would overwhelm the metrics system, so they belong in the log.

Telemetry is data about customers, so it falls under the same care as any other personal data. The rule is to keep what diagnosis needs, for as long as it needs it, and nothing more. In the prediction log, the customer identifier is stored as a keyed hash, so predictions can still be joined to outcomes and sliced by customer group, without storing the identifier itself. The delivery address is never logged, only the delivery zone, which is what the model uses, and the raw request body is not logged at all. Feature values are kept for ninety days, long enough for training-serving skew checks and for replaying requests during an investigation. Predictions and model versions are kept for thirteen months, so a year of quality can be joined to matured labels and compared with the same season. Alerts are divided by what should happen when they fire. A ninety-ninth percentile above a hundred and fifty milliseconds, or a fallback rate above two percent, pages the on-call engineer, because customers are affected now. A drift score above nought point two five, or a weekly log loss above nought point four, opens a ticket for the ML team, because it needs investigation, not a three a.m. response. And every alert has an owner, a runbook action, and an urgency.

The word drift covers several different kinds of change. They have different causes, and they do different things to model quality, so it helps to name them. Training-serving skew means the live inputs differ from training because of a bug or a contract break, like distances arriving in metres. It hurts immediately. A population shift means the mix of inputs changes while the relationship stays the same, like the lighter gift parcels of December. It is often harmless, because the model has seen such parcels before. A label shift means the outcome rate itself changes, as in a storm week where the late rate rises from nine to twenty-two percent. The ranking may still be fine, but the predicted risks are too low, so calibration suffers. A concept change means the same inputs now lead to different outcomes, as when a new carrier with different delays takes over some zones. It hurts slowly, as the old relationship stops holding. And a selection change means which outcomes are observed changes, for example when expedited orders stop producing a normal label. Then the labels themselves mislead, which chapter nine returns to. Every comparison also needs a reference. Training data shows what the model learned, but is old. The last four weeks are recent, but seasonal. The same week last year is the seasonal match.

A drift statistic measures how much a distribution moved. It says nothing at all about whether the move hurts the model. This section compares two changes using the population stability index, a common drift score computed over ten bins of the reference distribution, where values above nought point two five are usually treated as a significant shift. In week fifteen, one source starts sending distances in metres, affecting thirty percent of orders. The service stays up and predicts on nonsense distances, and the distance feature scores a stability index of nought point four six three. In December, parcels become lighter because of gift shopping, and the weight feature scores nought point five eight seven, the larger of the two. Both cross the alert line. Now look at quality, as production observation on matured labels. The metres problem raised the weekly log loss from nought point three nine four to nought point four seven one, breaching the quality contract. The December shift moved it from nought point three nine four to nought point three nine six, no real change. So the harmless shift scored higher than the harmful one. Two limits follow. A stable distribution of each feature does not prove stable quality, since concept change can leave every marginal unchanged. And the metres problem was caught most directly by a simple range rule.

Model quality in production is measured by joining predictions to their outcomes once the labels mature, and only for the orders that have a fair label. For week fourteen, the join runs seven days after checkout, covering eight thousand six hundred delivered orders, grouped by their predicted late risk. Where the model predicted five percent, four point eight percent were late. Where it predicted a quarter, twenty-five point one percent were late. At thirty-five percent predicted, thirty-six point two observed. At a half, fifty-one point six. These are well calibrated. But in the riskiest bucket, where the model predicted seventy percent, eighty point five percent were actually late. The riskiest orders are under-predicted, which matters because those are exactly the orders where the delivery window should widen most. The join's rules matter as much as its results. Delivered, matured orders are included. Orders checked out less than seven days ago are included later, once mature. Cancelled orders have no label and are counted separately. Orders that operations expedited are flagged, because that action changed the outcome the label records, a bias the next chapter examines. And quality is reported in slices, by risk bucket, zone and new customers, not as one average.

Here the chapter's two examples meet. Both alerts look alike at first: a service that is perfectly healthy by every operational measure, and a drift alert on one feature. Triage separates them before anyone retrains anything. In week fifteen, uptime, errors and latency are all healthy. The distance feature has a stability index of nought point four six, and the range rule shows thirty percent of distances above eighty kilometres. The same week last year shows no such shift, and once labels mature, log loss has risen from nought point three nine four to nought point four seven one. The diagnosis is training-serving skew: one source is sending metres. The response is a data fix: correct the source, quarantine the affected rows, and replay them. Retraining on the corrupt data would make things worse. In December the service is also healthy. The weight feature scores nought point five nine, but no rule is broken, the same shift happened last December, and quality is unchanged. The diagnosis is a seasonal population shift, and the response is to note it and do nothing more. The order of questions generalises. Is the change real, or a logging artefact? Where does it come from, one source or everyone? Does it hurt quality, by labels, slices and seasons? Only then, match the fix.

A deployed model generates evidence, but only if the system records what happened, in order, for every prediction. That takes four events per order, joined by one prediction identifier. The prediction event records what the model said: a risk of nought point six four from version fourteen, with the features it used. The exposure event records what the customer actually saw, a delivery window of three to five days, and which experiment arm they were in. The action event records what was done because of the prediction: here, operations expedited the order at twenty to four. And the outcome event records what followed: the parcel was delivered on day two, on time. The action event is the one most often missing, and it matters most. Without it, an on-time delivery for a high-risk order looks as though the model was simply wrong, and the next model learns that such orders are safe. With it, the outcome is read correctly, as the result of an intervention. So the action record says which action was taken, whether it was decided by a rule or a person, and when. It also says whether the order was in a small holdout group that is deliberately never acted on, which the next sections rely on.

A canary shows that a new version runs safely. To claim that the new delivery-window policy actually helps, reducing broken promises, needs a randomised comparison, planned before it starts. The unit is the customer, hashed and split fifty-fifty, so each customer sees one policy throughout. The primary metric is the broken-promise rate, and the experiment is sized to detect a fall from eight percent to seven. At the usual significance and power, that needs ten thousand eight hundred and eighty-seven orders per arm, inflated slightly, by a factor of one point nought seven five, because a customer's repeat orders are correlated. With a hundred and eighty thousand orders a day, that is only about three hours of traffic. But the calendar, not the sample size, decides how long to run. Order mix and delivery performance follow a weekly cycle, so the experiment runs for fourteen days, two full cycles, and is read out on day twenty-one, once the last orders' labels have matured. Guardrails, checkout conversion, support contacts and latency, can stop it early for harm. Two rules protect the conclusion. No peeking: stopping at day three because the number looks good greatly inflates false wins. And there is one primary metric; everything else is secondary.

Here the system's own success creates a problem. Operations expedite the orders that the model flags as high risk, and that changes the outcomes the next model will learn from. Consider the orders with a predicted risk above nought point six. Left alone, sixty percent of them would arrive late. Expedited, only fifteen percent do. Eighty percent of these orders are expedited, so in the training data the late rate for this group is twenty-four percent, not sixty. A model retrained on those labels learns that these orders are fairly safe, predicts lower risk, and stops flagging them, after which they stop being expedited, and the late rate climbs back. The model has undermined its own signal. Several fixes keep the labels honest. A small random holdout, five percent of flagged orders, about two hundred a week out of four thousand, is never expedited, so its late rate shows the true risk, around sixty percent. Logging the action, as in section one, lets training use only the orders that were not acted on, or include the action as a feature. Or the target can be redefined as the risk of lateness if not expedited. The general point holds for any deployed model: an action taken on a prediction biases the labels that follow.
