Retraining can be triggered in several ways, and each trigger should lead to a specific next step. Some should lead to investigation rather than to training. A schedule, the first of each month, trains a candidate and lets the gates from chapter five decide whether it is any better. A data trigger, a new month of matured labels arriving, does exactly the same. A drift alert, a stability index above nought point two five on some feature, should not start a retrain directly. It should start the triage from chapter eight, because a drift alert is often a data problem, not a model problem. A performance alert, weekly log loss above nought point four, should start a diagnosis too: retrain only if the cause turns out to be the model itself, for example concept change, rather than broken inputs. Week fifteen shows why. Retraining automatically on the distance drift would have produced a model trained on distances in metres, teaching it the bug, and making the eventual data fix break the model. And whatever starts it, continuous training is not continuous deployment. Training a candidate and running its gates can be fully automatic. Rolling it out still needs an approval and a canary, exactly as for any other change.

A retrain run today cannot use today's orders, because their labels have not matured yet, and including them would bias the model. So the training window must end where the labels are complete. For the May retrain, run on the first of May, training covers six months, from the first of November to the seventeenth of April. Six months includes a December, so the seasonal shift from chapter eight is represented. Validation uses the eighteenth to the twenty-fourth of April, the most recent week whose labels have all matured. The last six days of April are excluded entirely, because many of those orders have not yet reached their promised date plus three days. The holdout orders from section three are included, and flagged. It is worth seeing what goes wrong otherwise. If the window ran up to yesterday, the most recent orders would mostly appear on time, simply because their late deliveries have not happened yet. The model would learn a risk that is systematically too low, and look fine on any validation set built the same way. Finally, the window is computed from the run date by a function, and reads a named snapshot, so the candidate can be rebuilt exactly, as chapter three requires.

A retrained model is just another candidate. It goes through the same gates, the same approval and the same rollout as any other change to what serves. The path is the same every time. The pipeline retrains. The candidate is gated against the current champion, not against whichever model happened to be champion when the pipeline was written. It is registered as an immutable version. A person approves it, and that approval is recorded. A five percent canary runs. Only then does the champion alias move. Look at six months of monthly retrains. In January the candidate passed and became version twelve. In February the run stopped at the data gate, because of the metres problem in one source. In March the candidate showed no gain, so the champion stayed. In April, version thirteen failed on latency and rural recall, as chapter five showed, and a retuned version fourteen passed every gate and was promoted after a forty-eight hour canary. In May the comparison was inconclusive, so version fourteen stayed, and the team waited for another month of labels. Most of these retrains did not change what serves at all, and that is a healthy sign. A pipeline that promotes every month would be promoting noise.

Automated retraining adds state and concurrency, and with them, the possibility that two runs act on the same model at once. Here is a race on the champion alias. At ten o'clock pipeline A, the monthly retrain, reads the champion as version fourteen. A minute later pipeline B, a hotfix rebuild, also reads version fourteen. At ten twenty, A's candidate, version fifteen, passes its gates against fourteen. At ten twenty-two, B sets the champion to the hotfix, version fourteen point one. At ten twenty-five, A sets the champion to fifteen, blindly overwriting the alias, so the hotfix is silently lost, and fifteen was never compared against what it replaced. With a compare-and-set, A's update says it expects the champion to be fourteen. It finds fourteen point one instead, so the update is refused, and A must re-gate against the new champion. Other kinds of state need the same care. A warm start, training from the previous model's weights, saves time but inherits that model's biases. Duplicate triggers are absorbed by the run key from chapter four. And an incremental fit makes the previous model an input to the next, so it needs to be versioned like any other input. The guard is simple: promote only if the champion is still the version you compared against.

A maintenance review does not have to end in an update. It can end in one of four ways, and not updating, or retiring, are decisions with their own evidence. Update, when a candidate passes every gate, as version fourteen did in April. Wait, when the comparison is inconclusive or there are too few matured labels to decide, as in May, when version fourteen stayed and the team gathered another month. No change, when the investigated shift is harmless, like the December parcels: recording that decision is part of the work. And retire, when the decision no longer needs a model at all. Suppose the main carrier starts providing its own delivery windows, which are more accurate because the carrier sees its own network. Retiring the late-risk model then has an order to it. First move every caller, so checkout uses the carrier's window, and confirm nothing else still calls the predictor. Then stop materialising its features, but only once no other model reads them. Turn off the retraining pipeline's schedule and the monitoring jobs, so they do not page anyone about a model nobody uses. And let the prediction logs and training snapshots expire under their retention rules from chapters five and eight, rather than keeping them forever by default.

Every step of the ML lifecycle runs as some identity, a person or a service, and access control starts by deciding what each identity may do. Each one gets only what its step needs, and no single identity can both train a model and deploy it. In the grid, ML engineers can read labels and train models, but only in the development environment. They cannot register a production model, move an alias or deploy. The training pipeline, a service identity, reads labels, trains and registers candidate versions. A release approver, a person, can move the champion alias, and does nothing else in this list. The continuous delivery system deploys. The serving pods themselves can do none of these things: they only read the model and features they need to answer requests. Analysts see aggregates, never the raw labels of individual customers. Four principles sit behind the grid. Least privilege: each identity holds only what its step requires, so a leaked credential can do limited harm. Separation of duties: whoever trains cannot also deploy, so no single mistake or bad actor can push a model to customers alone. Machines do the routine steps and people approve them, which keeps approvals meaningful. And every environment has its own identities, so staging credentials never work in production.

Security controls for an ML service start with three questions: which network paths exist at all, where secrets live, and what is encrypted. On the network side, only the checkout API can call the predictor, which runs in a private subnet with no public address. The serving pods can read the online feature store, read-only, and read the model registry when they start. They write logs to a sink they can write to but not read from. And outbound access to the internet is denied entirely, so even a compromised pod cannot send data out or download anything. On secrets, the feature-store token lives in a secret manager, is mounted into the pod when it starts, and is rotated automatically every thirty days. Access to the registry needs no stored secret at all, because it uses workload identity: the platform vouches for the pod's identity directly. And CI scans both code and images, so a secret that slips into either fails the build. On encryption, data at rest is encrypted with keys held in a key management service, and data in transit uses TLS, including traffic inside the cluster, rather than trusting the internal network. None of this is specific to ML. That is the point: an ML service gets the same controls as any other service.

Data minimisation means every field in an ML system is kept because a named use needs it, in the least detail that use requires, and with an end date set when it first enters the system. The data inventory for the late-risk lifecycle makes this concrete. The delivery address is not needed by the model, which uses the delivery zone, so only the zone is copied into ML systems, and the address stays in the order system that owns it. The customer identifier is needed for joins and for repeat-customer features, so it is kept, but as a keyed hash. Order history is needed for the customer late rate feature, so only aggregates are kept, over a rolling twelve months. Phone numbers and email addresses have no use in modelling at all, so they never enter the ML systems. Prediction logs keep hashed identifiers for thirteen months, for quality joins and audits. The inventory also records decisions not to collect. A proposal to use customer support transcripts as a feature was rejected, because no expected gain justified bringing free-text personal conversations into the training data. So any new field has to pass three tests: a named use, the least detail that serves it, and an end date.

When a customer asks for their data to be deleted, lineage is what makes the request answerable, because it shows every place that data was copied to. Deleting the rows, though, does not remove their influence on models already trained. Trace one request. On the twelfth of May the customer's fourteen orders are deleted from the warehouse, and their row in the online feature store is removed. On the thirteenth, thirty-one prediction events are deleted from the logs, found by the hashed key. Lineage then shows that the customer's orders appear in three training snapshots, which are rewritten without them by the twentieth. And lineage shows that models version twelve and version fourteen were trained on those snapshots. Those models still carry a small influence from this customer's data. Deleting the source rows cannot reach inside a fitted model. The practical options are to retrain without the deleted rows, which here happens at the June retrain. Methods that claim to make a model unlearn specific examples exist, but they are approximate and need specialist review. Either way, record which models still carry the influence, and until when. None of this would be possible without lineage: the snapshots and models trained on the deleted data could not even be found.

Every package, container image and model file in an ML system is an input that someone else wrote or built, so each one needs a check that it is exactly what you think it is. Python packages are pinned with hashes and installed from an internal mirror, so a typo-squatted name or a hijacked release cannot slip in. Base images come only from an allow-listed registry, with their signatures verified. The serving image is signed by CI after it is built and tested, and the signature is verified again at deploy time, so an image swapped after testing is refused. Model files use a safe format, and their hash is recorded in the manifest, as chapter five required. Pretrained weights, which come from outside entirely, have their source, licence and hash recorded before use. In CI, installing with required hashes means that any package file that differs from the recorded hash fails the install. A software bill of materials records what is inside every image, so a newly announced vulnerability can be traced to the images that contain it. And the cluster's admission policy accepts only images signed with the CI key. Unsafe deserialisation deserves one rule of its own: never load a pickle file you did not build, because loading it can run any code its author chose.

A threat model asks three things: what is valuable, who might want to attack it, and through which input. For most ML services, baseline controls cover most cases, and a few need security specialists. Five threats to the late-risk system illustrate the range. Credential theft, such as a leaked registry token, is handled by workload identity and rotation, ordinary security hygiene. Data poisoning means feeding in fake orders to shift a zone's predicted risk, perhaps to manipulate delivery windows. The source checks, quarantine rules and the random holdout from earlier chapters all make that harder, and a targeted attack would need specialist analysis. Model extraction means scraping many delivery windows to reconstruct the model, which rate limits and deliberately coarse outputs, a window rather than a precise probability, make expensive. Membership inference asks whether a particular customer was in the training data. Using aggregate features rather than raw identifiers helps, but assessing it properly is a specialist question. Insider misuse, such as reading one customer's raw labels, is handled by access audits and least privilege. The orientation questions generalise: what is valuable, the data, the model or the decisions it drives? Who would attack, through which input, and at what cost? And when does the risk go beyond baseline controls?

Governance documentation is useful only if it stays true, so it records decisions and limits, and it is reviewed on a schedule. It is evidence that supports judgement, not a certificate. The risk record for the late-risk model starts with its intended use: setting the delivery window at checkout. It also says what it must not be used for: not pricing, and not refusing orders. Its known limits are listed plainly: rural recall of nought point seven four, weaker performance for new delivery stations, and storm weeks. Exceptions are recorded with an expiry date and an owner. Here, raw zone delay logs are being kept for a hundred and twenty days instead of ninety, while an investigation finishes, and that exception expires on the thirtieth of June. The record is reviewed quarterly, or whenever something material changes. Access is reviewed on the same cycle. The second-quarter review covered forty-two grants. Thirty were used within the last ninety days and correctly scoped, so they stay. Seven had not been used for ninety days, so they are revoked. Five were broader than the role needs, so they are narrowed. And it is worth saying plainly what all of this is not. A risk record and an access review are not a compliance certificate.

Legal and regulatory obligations depend on where a model is used and how it is used, so the team's job has a clear boundary. The team prepares accurate, current evidence. Specialists in privacy, legal and compliance judge what applies. Four kinds of obligation are common. Data protection raises questions about the lawful basis for processing, and about customers' rights to access and delete their data. Rules on automated decisions ask whether a model decides something significant about a person without human involvement. Consumer law asks whether what the customer is promised, here a delivery window, is fair and accurate. And sector-specific or AI-specific rules may impose their own requirements, depending on the jurisdiction and the domain. For each, the team prepares the evidence that the specialists will need. That means the data inventory, the lineage and the deletion traces. It means the intended use, written down, along with any human override, such as operations staff who can change a window. And it means the quality evidence, such as calibration and the broken-promise rate. The specialists then decide, jurisdiction by jurisdiction. A new use of the model, such as feeding its risk into pricing, means a new review. And this course offers orientation, not legal advice.

Capacity is estimated from the shape of demand and a few stated assumptions, and then checked against what is actually measured. The checkout predictor's demand follows the shopping day. It averages twelve requests a second, falls almost to nothing overnight, and peaks at forty requests a second at seven in the evening. A sale day is assumed to triple that peak, to a hundred and twenty. That is an assumption, written down, not a forecast anyone has proved. One replica can handle about a hundred and thirty-three requests a second, from the queueing analysis in chapter seven, but it is run at fifty percent utilisation, about sixty-seven requests a second, to stay well left of the latency knee. And the fleet must survive losing one of its two availability zones, which means each zone must be able to carry the whole peak alone. On a normal day the peak fits on one replica at fifty percent, so two replicas, one per zone, survive a zone loss. On a sale day the peak needs two replicas, so four are needed to survive a zone loss. Autoscaling then follows the daily curve, while the minimum replica count covers the zone loss. None of this is a benchmark. When the model or its features change, the per-replica capacity is measured again.

Every component that can fail takes a different share of the system with it, so reliability planning goes domain by domain, and decides in advance the order in which the service degrades. A single pod failing takes out one replica of four, and readiness probes simply route around it while it restarts. A node failing takes out the pods on it, which is why pods are spread across nodes. A zone failing takes out half the fleet, covered by the zone-safe sizing from the previous section. The feature store failing affects every single prediction, which is why the labelled fallback window exists. And the model registry failing means new pods cannot load a model, so each node caches the current bundle, and pods that are already running keep serving. Cold starts matter most during a surge. If load rises from forty to a hundred and twenty requests a second in two minutes, the autoscaler asks for more replicas within about thirty seconds, but a new node takes around ninety seconds to provision, and a pod fourteen more to become ready. Until that capacity arrives, the service sheds load above seventy percent utilisation to the fallback window, rather than letting every request slow down. The degradation order is fixed: first skip optional features, then shed the excess load, and only as a last resort answer every request with rules.

A more accurate model usually costs more to run, so put a price on each option, at the same latency contract, and attribute the bill to the model that causes it. The checkout predictor handles thirty-one million one hundred and four thousand calls a month, and a replica is assumed to cost eighteen pence an hour. Version fourteen, a gradient-boosted model of three hundred trees, meets the ninety-ninth percentile contract on four replicas, about five hundred and eighteen pounds a month, or under two pence per thousand calls. Version thirteen, the larger ensemble from chapter five, needs eight replicas to meet the same latency, about one thousand and thirty-seven pounds a month. And it is better by just five ten-thousandths of log loss. Read together, that is twice the cost for a gain that sits inside the run-to-run noise measured in chapter three. It would only be worth paying if the gain moved the product objective, fewer broken delivery promises, and that can only be shown by an experiment, not by the offline score. Making these trade-offs visible needs cost attribution. Serving replicas are charged to the late-risk model in each environment, feature-store reads to each model by read count, training runs to the pipeline's run key, and logs and storage to their owning model by volume.

The choice of serving platform is mostly a choice about what the team must own and operate itself. The guide is to pick the smallest one that meets the contract. A managed endpoint, run by a cloud provider, leaves the team owning the model and its configuration and little more. With a minimum number of replicas set, it has no cold starts, and each endpoint is isolated from the others. An own cluster gives full control, but the team then owns the nodes, the autoscaling and every upgrade as well, and that only pays off with many models and a platform team to run them. A serverless function owns the least of all, but starts new instances on demand, with cold starts of seconds, which is a poor fit for a strict ninety-ninth percentile at checkout, though fine for spiky, latency-tolerant work. For this retailer today, with one or two models and a small team, a managed endpoint is the sensible choice, and an own cluster becomes worth considering if the number of models multiplies. A few questions decide it. Who will run it at three in the morning, by name? Does it meet the contract on latency, isolation and cost? And how hard would it be to leave? Keeping the bundle itself portable, as chapter five required, keeps that option open.

A backup only counts once it has been restored. Each store gets two objectives, and a drill that proves them. The recovery point objective says how much data may be lost, how old the latest usable backup may be. The recovery time objective says how long a restore may take before the system must be working again. The second-quarter drill restored each store into an empty staging account, as though the original were gone. The model registry and its bundles were restored in twenty-five minutes, against a target of one hour, a pass. The offline feature store failed entirely: the role used for restoring could not decrypt the backup, because the key permissions had never been granted to it. Prediction logs were restored in six hours, inside their twenty-four hour target. And the split manifests were restored, but two of the identifier files they referenced were missing, so a model could not have been rebuilt from them, which counts as a fail. So two of four restores failed, and neither failure had been noticed before the drill, because the backups themselves had been running and reporting success every night. The lesson is that permissions and keys are part of the backup. Both failures were fixed, and will be drilled again next quarter.

Here is an incident of the kind ML systems are prone to. Every service was green for three days while the model's predictions were wrong. At two in the morning on Monday, the carrier's feed switched its delivered-at timestamps from universal time to local time, an hour ahead. Every timestamp still parsed, so nothing failed. But the zone delay feature, the average delay over the last three hours, rose by about sixty minutes in every zone. Predicted late risk was inflated across the board, and around forty percent more customers were shown wider delivery windows. Latency, errors and uptime stayed perfect. Model quality could not see it either, because labels take seven days to mature. On Wednesday at half past ten, the checkout conversion guardrail showed a drop of one point four percent against the previous week, and opened a ticket. By ten past eleven, triage had found a large shift in zone delay with no seasonal match, and the incident was declared severity two, because customers were affected. At twenty-five past, the team contained it by pinning zone delay to Sunday's medians, labelled as such. And by two o'clock the fix was in: converting to universal time at ingest, and replaying every feature since Monday. Throughout, one incident lead decided and communicated, containment came before root cause, and the evidence was kept.

Recovery has three parts: repair the cause, replay whatever the cause touched, and accept what has already happened in the world. For this incident, the repair converts delivered-at to universal time at ingest, so new features are correct from now on. The replay recomputes the feature history since Monday, so training data built from that period is correct too. It is worth asking whether to roll the model back, and the answer here is no. The model was fine; its input was wrong, so rolling back to version twelve would have fed the same wrong input to an older model. Open orders that have not been delivered yet are re-scored, so their windows are correct from now on. Then the parts that cannot be undone. The windows shown to customers from Monday to Wednesday stay shown. Some of those customers abandoned checkout because of a wider window, and those orders are not recovered. Whether to contact or compensate anyone is a product decision, not an engineering one, and it should be made deliberately rather than ignored. One more decision falls to the postmortem: what to do with the Monday to Wednesday rows in the next retrain. Their features have been replayed, but their outcomes were shaped by the wrong windows, so they are excluded or flagged.

A postmortem turns an incident into changes. Written blamelessly, it asks what made the failure possible and what made it slow to see, rather than who made a mistake, and it turns each finding into a change with an owner and a date. Four factors contributed here. The carrier feed's contract had no timezone field, so switching to local time was a perfectly valid change by the contract's own terms. There was no rule on sudden jumps in the zone delay feature, so a sixty-minute step everywhere passed silently. Model quality metrics depend on matured labels, which leaves seven days in which they cannot see anything. And the conversion guardrail took two days to fire, because conversion is noisy from day to day. Each becomes an action. To prevent it, timestamps in the feed contract must carry an explicit offset, owned by data engineering, due at the end of June. To detect it sooner, an alert on any step of more than twenty minutes in the zone delay medians, and a daily check of the model's score distribution against the previous week, both owned by the ML team. To contain it next time, a runbook step for pinning a feature to its medians, already done. And the actions are tracked until they are done, not just written down.

This final chapter reviews the whole lifecycle as one design, and that review starts with a map: what exists, what depends on what, and who owns each piece. The retailer runs two systems, kept deliberately apart. The checkout predictor runs inside every checkout: the checkout team's API calls the late-risk model, version fourteen, owned by the ML team, which reads online features maintained by the data platform team. The daily planning job runs overnight: data engineering's one o'clock snapshot feeds the duration model, version nine, whose scores the logistics team's routing system reads. Between them sit shared pieces: the carrier's delivery scans, which supply the labels, the retraining pipeline, and the model registry run by the ML platform. Every arrow on that map is a contract with an owner. A request and response within a hundred and fifty milliseconds at the ninety-ninth percentile. Features no more than fifteen minutes old. Scores for every zone published by five in the morning. And, since the incident in chapter eleven, a scan feed whose timestamps carry an explicit offset from universal time. Keeping separate contracts for the two systems matters, because they fail differently, change at different rates and are judged by different people, so one shared, blurred contract would fit neither.

Behind each serving model there should be an unbroken chain of identities, running from the data it learned from to the release record that put it live. For the late-risk model, version fourteen, the chain runs from the orders snapshot, version three, through a split manifest with its fingerprint, the checkout features at version six, and the training run with its own identifier, to a bundle with a recorded hash, and finally to the release record. The evidence attached is the gate report, which passed, and the canary, whose guardrails held. The duration model, version nine, has the same chain with different links. It is trained from the nightly one o'clock snapshot and the planning features at version three, and has no labelled split in the same sense, since its evaluation uses completed routes. Its evidence is a gate pass, followed by a seven-night shadow run alongside the previous version. The chain is only useful if it is checked rather than assumed. A short script walks it end to end. It checks that the hash of the bundle being served matches the hash in the approved release. It checks that the run's split fingerprint matches the split manifest it names. And it checks that the training snapshot still exists, so the model could still be rebuilt, which chapter three showed can quietly stop being true.

The clearest test of a lifecycle design is to follow one change all the way through it. Here is the late-risk model, version fourteen, from new data to full traffic. At three in the morning on the first of April, the monthly pipeline retrains from a window that ends where labels are matured. By ten past four, the data and evaluation gates have passed, and at quarter past, version fourteen is registered as an immutable version with its lineage. On the second, staging loads it against the staging feature store, the signature is validated, and a load test shows a ninety-ninth percentile of a hundred and twenty-one milliseconds. On the third, at twelve minutes past nine, a release approver signs it off, and the approval is recorded. From the third to the fifth, it runs first in shadow and then as a five percent canary assigned by customer, and every guardrail holds. At half past nine on the fifth the champion alias moves, the pods reload, and responses start carrying version fourteen. From the twelfth onwards, once labels mature, weekly quality reports follow. Just as important are the exits. A gate could have failed or been inconclusive. Staging could have revealed a latency or loading problem. And the canary could have breached a guardrail. Each exit is a normal outcome, not a failure of the process.

The two systems run under different policies, and writing them side by side makes the differences deliberate rather than accidental. The checkout predictor's service objective is ninety-nine point nine percent of requests answered well within a hundred and fifty milliseconds, over thirty days. Its quality check is a weekly log loss of at most nought point four, on matured labels. Drift is watched with stability scores and range rules against a seasonal reference. Feedback is kept honest by the five percent holdout of flagged orders that are never expedited. It produces a gated candidate every month, and promotion needs an approval and a forty-eight hour canary. The daily planning job's objective is different in kind: scores published by five in the morning on ninety-nine percent of nights. Its quality check is a weekly mean absolute error in predicted duration of at most nought point six hours. It retrains quarterly, and promotion needs an approval and a seven-night shadow run, since a canary would split one night's routing plan in two. The differences have reasons. Risk labels take seven days to mature, while duration is known the day after delivery. A bad checkout prediction harms customers directly, while a bad plan is seen first by planners. And the checkout model changes monthly, the planning model quarterly.

A good lifecycle review does two things. It shows the evidence that the controls actually work, and it names plainly the risks that remain, each with an owner and a next step. On file is the second-quarter access review, which revoked seven grants and narrowed five. The restore drill, in which two of four restores failed, both now fixed, with a repeat drill due next quarter. A rollback to version twelve, restored and tested in staging on the second of April. And continuous enforcement that only signed images are admitted to the cluster. Five risks remain open. Feedback bias: the unexpedited holdout is small, about two hundred orders a week, so estimates for the riskiest orders are noisy, and its size will be reviewed. Rural recall is nought point seven four, close to its floor of nought point seven, and needs more rural data. The feed-contract fix from the incident, timestamps with explicit offsets, is not live yet and is due at the end of June. Labels remain blind for seven days after any change, which the new daily score checks only partly cover. And the carrier's own delivery windows may make the model unnecessary, a retirement decision for product. Finally, an honest note: this is a design review, built from supplied traces, not evidence of having operated the system.

The design in this course is deliberately small, and the last question is when it should grow. The answer is that each larger capability waits for a signal that would justify the cost of running it. Today there is one online feature store with two feature views. A full shared feature platform becomes worth it when several teams start sharing features. There is one pipeline per model, and a shared orchestration layer becomes worth it with many models that share steps. Serving uses a managed endpoint, to be reviewed if the number of models reaches five. Experiments are planned and analysed by hand, and dedicated tooling makes sense once tests run every month. Streaming features are not built at all, and should only be built if a use appears that needs freshness under a minute, which the late-risk model does not. What carries over to any system, at any size, is a set of habits. Contracts, each with an owner. Identities for everything that can change a result. Gates and rollouts that are allowed to stop. Fallbacks that say they are fallbacks. And evidence labelled for exactly what it is.
